# Concepts

## Introduction

> Simulation is the act of creating, artificially, possible paths (behavior) of a system subject to uncertainty [@brooks2014introductory].

. . .

- Any system of stochastic (random) equations can be simulated with code (and R)

. . .

- Applications of simulation in empirical problems (including Finance) are widespread

## Calculating pi

Estimating a deterministic quantity with random draws (Monte Carlo):

$$P(\text{point inside the circle}) = \frac{\pi}{4} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \hat{\pi} = 4 \times \frac{\text{hits}}{M}$$

{{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/ELetCV_wX_c?si=xXHg7oHbFxMXM0h3 aspect-ratio="4x3" width="700" title='Approximating PI (Monte Carlo Integration)' >}}


## Calculating pi - animation

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: pi-anim
#| fig-cap: "Each dot is one random draw; the estimate is 4 × (dots inside the circle) / total."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-dpi: 110

gif_file <- "figs/pi_animation.gif"

if (!file.exists(gif_file)) {
  local({
    suppressPackageStartupMessages({
      library(gganimate)
      library(dplyr)
    })

    set.seed(172)
    N <- 4000      # total number of random draws
    per <- 50      # new draws per animation frame
    fps <- 12

    draws <- data.frame(i = 1:N,
                        x = runif(N, -1, 1),
                        y = runif(N, -1, 1))
    draws$inside <- factor(ifelse(draws$x^2 + draws$y^2 <= 1, "Dentro", "Fora"),
                           levels = c("Dentro", "Fora"))
    draws$est <- 4 * cumsum(draws$inside == "Dentro") / draws$i
    draws$frame <- ceiling(draws$i / per)

    frames <- unique(draws$frame)

    # one row per frame: the running estimate shown in the text box
    lab <- data.frame(frame = frames, i = frames * per) |>
      mutate(est = draws$est[i],
             txt = sprintf("n = %s\n\u03c0\u0302 \u2248 %s",
                           format(i, big.mark = ".", decimal.mark = ","),
                           format(round(est, 4), nsmall = 4, decimal.mark = ",")))

    # frame-stacked data: everything drawn up to each frame
    df <- bind_rows(lapply(frames, function(f) {
      d <- draws[draws$frame <= f, c("i", "x", "y", "inside")]
      d$frame <- f
      d
    }))

    p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
      annotate("rect", xmin = -1, xmax = 1, ymin = -1, ymax = 1,
               fill = "grey97", color = "grey40") +
      annotate("path",
               x = cos(seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 400)),
               y = sin(seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = 400)),
               color = "grey20", linewidth = .8) +
      geom_point(aes(color = inside), size = 1.1, alpha = .7, stroke = 0) +
      geom_label(data = lab, aes(x = -0.94, y = 0.95, label = txt),
                 inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
                 fill = "white", color = "grey20", linewidth = .25,
                 label.r = unit(.15, "lines"), family = "mono",
                 fontface = "bold", size = 4.2, lineheight = .95) +
      scale_color_manual(values = c("Dentro" = "#1667c4", "Fora" = "grey60"),
                         name = NULL) +
      guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 3.5, alpha = 1))) +
      coord_fixed(xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1), expand = FALSE) +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
      theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
            axis.text = element_blank(),
            axis.title = element_blank(),
            legend.position = "bottom",
            legend.key.size = unit(.9, "lines"),
            plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
            plot.title.position = "plot",
            plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)) +
      labs(title = "Estimando \u03c0 com sorteios aleat\u00f3rios") +
      transition_manual(frame)

    anim_save(gif_file, p, nframes = length(frames), fps = fps,
              renderer = gifski_renderer())
  })
}

knitr::include_graphics(gif_file)
```

## Steps for a simulation

1. Define or estimate a mathematical structure of the data generating process;

. . .

2. Simulate the system of equations a reasonable amount of times and save the measure of interest at the end of each simulation;

. . .

3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 many times;


# Simulating with R

## Random sampling in R


We always assume that the distribution of the random variables is known (or approximated by):
		
- Symmetric: Uniform, Normal, Student's t, Beta, etc
- Positive: exponential, Gamma, Weibull, etc
- Many more

In R, every distribution has a `r` function: `rnorm()`, `runif()`, `rgamma()`, `rbeta()`, ...


## Random sampling in R - Examples {.scrollable}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Normal Distribution

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
# Normal variable
X <- rnorm(n = N, mean = 0, sd = 1)

ggplot(data.frame(X), aes(x = X)) + geom_histogram() + 
  labs(title = 'Normal Distribution') + 
  theme_light()

```

### Gamma

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
# Gamma variable
X <- rgamma(n = N, shape = 1)

ggplot(data.frame(X), aes(x = X)) + 
        geom_histogram() + labs(title = 'Gamma') + 
  theme_light()

```

### Uniform

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
# Uniform variable
X <- runif(n = N)

ggplot(data.frame(X), aes(x = X)) + 
        geom_histogram() + labs(title = 'Uniform') + 
  theme_light()
```

### Beta

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
# Beta variable
X <- rbeta(n = N, shape1 = 0.5, shape2 = 0.5)

ggplot(data.frame(X), aes(x = X)) + 
        geom_histogram() + labs(title = 'Beta') + 
  theme_light()
```

:::


## How many simulations are enough?

Each simulation result is an **estimate**: it changes if you change the seed. Its precision is measured by the **Monte Carlo standard error**:

$$SE(\hat{\theta}) = \frac{SD\left(\hat{\theta}_i\right)}{\sqrt{M}}$$

. . .

- Quadrupling `M` only halves the error: accuracy is expensive
- The estimate is ~95% within $\pm 1.96 \times SE$ of the true value
- Always report the estimate **and** its Monte Carlo error


## Convergence in practice

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Estimate: 3.129 | Monte Carlo error: 0.023 | True value: 3.1416"
set.seed(1)
M <- 5000

# share of random points inside the unit circle, times 4
u1 <- runif(M)
u2 <- runif(M)
hit <- 4 * (u1^2 + u2^2 <= 1)

# running estimate and its standard error
est <- cumsum(hit) / seq_len(M)
se <- sqrt(cumsum((hit - est)^2) / (seq_len(M) - 1)) / sqrt(seq_len(M))

ggplot(data.frame(x = seq_len(M), est, se), aes(x = x, y = est)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = est - 1.96*se, ymax = est + 1.96*se), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = pi, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(2.6, 3.7)) +
  theme_light() +
  labs(title = "Monte Carlo estimate of pi",
       subtitle = "dashed line = true value (3.1416)",
       x = "Number of simulations (M)", y = "Estimate")
```


## A simple regression model

$y _i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \epsilon _i$

. . . 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Simulated data (points) and the fitted regression line"
N <- 100
alpha <- 10
beta <- 0.2

x <- rnorm(N, 100, 15)
eps <- rnorm(N, 0, 3)
y <- alpha + beta*x + eps

ggplot(data.frame(x, y), aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_light() +
  labs(x = "Regressor (x)", y = "Dependent (y)")
```


## A simple stochastic process in Finance
	
The discrete _Random Walk_ Model

\begin{eqnarray}
P_t&=&P_{t-1} \exp (R_t) \\
R_t &=& C + \epsilon _t \\
\epsilon _t &\sim& N\left(0,\sigma ^2 \right) 
\end{eqnarray}

where $P_t$ is the price of the contract, $R_t$ is the return (daily, monthly, ..)
		
A bit of math shows that:

- Since $E(R_t)=C$, you cannot predict $P_{t+1}$
- Since $\sigma(R_t)=\sigma(\epsilon _t)$, variance (uncertainty) per period is constant and increases with forecasting horizon

```{r, echo=FALSE}
i_exerc <- 1
```

# Applications

## Pricing European Options with Simulation
	
A call option of the European type is a financial contract where the payoff is a function of the spot price:

\begin{equation}
Payoff^C _T = \max(0 , P_T - K) 
\end{equation}
	
$Payoff^C _T$ - Payoff (payment) of call option

$P_T$ - Price of underlying asset in maturity ($T$)

$K$ - Strike price of contract

## Pricing the option with simulation

We can calculate the price (Expected payoff) of this call option by simulating stock prices and calculating the simulated payoff at the expiration date

$$C = \frac{E\left[Payoff_T\right]}{(1+r)^T}$$

where $r$ is the discount rate per period. With continuous compounding, $C = e^{-rT} E\left[Payoff_T\right]$.

::: {.callout-note}
The simulated prices use a zero drift ($C = 0$), i.e. we are assuming the risk-neutral measure.
:::

```{r, echo=FALSE}
i_exerc <- i_exerc + 1
```
## Exercise `r i_exerc` - Pricing a Call option {.scrollable}

Consider the following RW model

\begin{eqnarray}
R_t &=& 0 +  \epsilon _t \\
\epsilon _t &\sim& N\left(0, \sigma ^2 \right) \\
P_t&=&P_{t-1} \exp (R_t) \\
P_0 &=& 100 \\
\sigma &=& 0.015
\end{eqnarray}

1. Calculate the price of the call option with maturity in 100 periods, strike price equal to 110, yield rate equal to 5% for the whole time period. Use `set.seed(10)` and 1000 simulations
		
2. Price an European put option that matures in 100 periods, strike price equal to 90, with 1000 simulations and `set.seed(15)`
		

## Solution - Pricing the call option {.scrollable}

```{r}
#| echo: true
set.seed(10)

M <- 1000; nT <- 100
P_0 <- 100; sigma <- 0.015
K <- 110; r <- 0.05

R <- matrix(rnorm(M*nT, 0, sigma), M, nT)
P_T <- P_0 * exp(rowSums(R))
C <- mean(pmax(P_T - K, 0))/(1 + r)
C
```

The result is deterministic given the seed. Change the seed (or `M`) and the last digits will change.


```{r, echo=FALSE}
i_exerc <- i_exerc + 1
```

## Performance Analysis with Simulation (monkey trading) {visibility="hidden"}

![The help desk that trades for you](figs/sasktel_help_desk.jpg)	

Consider a trading strategy of any kind, using past prices or other information to create a trading signal, buy or sell. 
	
After implementing the strategy in the data, it will generate a total return at the end of the trading period
	
**One way** of testing if a trading strategy has potential is to compare it to random portfolios created by sampling trading signals randomly. That is, we use random signals to trade and check whether that approach can result in similar return to our strategy or not

\end{equation}
		
where $w_i$ is a random variable between 0 and 1 (function `runif()`)

# Bootstrap

## Bootstrapping standard errors

One of the outputs of a linear regression is the standard error of each coefficient.

Consider a scenario where we are interested in a transformation of the parameters, such as:

\begin{eqnarray}
y_t &=&  \alpha + \beta _1 x_{1,t} + \beta _2 x_{2,t} + \epsilon _t \\
\Theta &=& \frac{\beta _1 - \beta _2}{\alpha} 
\end{eqnarray}		
		
		
**How to find the standard error of $\Theta$?**
				
## Bootstrapping standard errors
	
1. Estimate the original model and save the created (conditional mean,  $\hat{y}_t$) and the vector of residuals, $\hat{\epsilon}_t$
		
2. Create a second variable $y^*$ given by:
		
\begin{equation}
y^*_t = \hat{y}_t + \epsilon ^* _t
\end{equation}
		
where $\epsilon ^* _t$ is a resampled vector of $\hat{\epsilon}_t$ (same size, with replacement: `sample(res, replace = TRUE)`)

---

3. Estimate the econometric model:

$$y ^* _t =  \alpha ^* + \beta ^* _1 x_{1,t} + \beta ^* _2 x_{2,t} + \epsilon _t $$
		
4. Calculate: 

$$\Theta ^* = \frac{\beta ^* _1 - \beta ^*  _2}{\alpha ^*} $$
		
5. Repeat steps 2, 3 and 4 `M` times, saving $\Theta ^*$ in each case
		
6. The final result will be a vector of $\Theta ^*$. Its standard error is simply the standard deviation of the vector


```{r, echo=FALSE}
i_exerc <- i_exerc + 1
```
